title: Real-Time Communication
tagline: Polling, long polling, SSE, and WebSockets — how servers push updates to clients for chat, feeds, and live data.
summary: Polling vs long-polling vs SSE vs WebSockets, and when to use each.

paragraphs: Normal HTTP is request/response — the *client* asks, the *server* answers. But chat, notifications, live scores, collaborative editors, and dashboards need the *server* to push data to the client the moment something happens. There are four common techniques to bridge that gap, from crude to purpose-built.

items.detail: Client repeatedly asks 'anything new?' on a timer (e.g., every 5 s). Dead simple, works everywhere, but wasteful (mostly empty responses) and laggy (updates wait for the next poll).

Client sends a request and the server *holds it open* until there's data (or a timeout), then responds; the client immediately re-requests. Near-real-time using plain HTTP, but ties up a connection per client and has reconnect overhead.

A single long-lived HTTP connection over which the *server streams* events to the client (one-directional, server→client). Built-in auto-reconnect, simple, great for feeds/notifications/live updates. Client→server still uses normal requests.

A persistent, *full-duplex* TCP connection — both sides can send anytime over one upgraded connection. The right tool for truly bidirectional, low-latency apps: chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing.

rows: One-way streams: notifications, feeds, live metrics
Two-way real-time: chat, games, collab editing

blocks.text: Decision rule: one-way server→client updates → SSE (simpler, auto-reconnects, plays well with HTTP/CDNs). Two-way, low-latency, frequent → WebSockets. Don't reach for WebSockets if SSE or even long polling suffices — they add stateful-connection complexity.

paragraphs: WebSockets/SSE introduce a new challenge: connections are **stateful and long-lived**, so a user is pinned to a specific server for the duration. That breaks the simple stateless model. Key concerns:

items.detail: Dedicate a tier of 'gateway'/connection servers that just hold WebSocket connections. Each can hold tens/hundreds of thousands of connections (limited by memory and file descriptors).

items.term: Routing messages to the right server
items.detail: User A on server 1 messages user B on server 7. You need a way to find B's server — a presence/registry (e.g., in Redis: user → connected server) and a pub/sub or message bus to forward the message to B's connection server.
LBs must support sticky, long-lived connections; you balance by connection count, not request rate.
Networks drop. Clients must reconnect and fetch anything missed while offline (store undelivered messages and replay on reconnect).

blocks.text: This 'connection server + presence registry + pub/sub fan-out' pattern is exactly what powers chat systems — you'll see it again in the WhatsApp/Messenger case study.

cheatsheet: HTTP is client-initiated; real-time needs server push — 4 options from crude to purpose-built.
Short polling (simple/wasteful) → long polling (held request) → SSE (server→client stream) → WebSockets (full-duplex).
One-way updates → SSE; two-way low-latency → WebSockets. Don't over-reach for WebSockets.
WebSocket/SSE connections are stateful & long-lived → users pinned to a connection server.
Scale with a connection-server tier + a presence registry (user→server in Redis) + pub/sub to route messages; handle reconnection/missed messages.

questions.prompt: For a live sports score ticker that only pushes updates to viewers, would you use WebSockets or SSE? Why?
answer: SSE is the better fit. The data flows only one way — server to client — and SSE is purpose-built for that: a single long-lived HTTP stream of events, with automatic reconnection built into the browser API, and it works nicely with standard HTTP infrastructure. You don't need the full-duplex capability of WebSockets, which would add unnecessary connection-management complexity.

Use WebSockets when the client also needs to send frequent low-latency messages back (chat, multiplayer, collaborative editing). Choosing the simpler tool that meets the requirement is itself a good signal.
keyPoints: SSE fits one-way streaming + auto-reconnect + HTTP-friendly
WebSockets are overkill without bidirectional needs
followUps: What happens to an SSE client that loses connectivity for 30 seconds?

questions.prompt: In a chat app, user A (connected to server 1) sends a message to user B (connected to server 7). How does the message reach B in real time?
questions.hint: Server 1 has no direct connection to B. How does it find and reach B's server?
answer: Server 1 doesn't hold B's connection, so it must locate B's connection server and forward the message there. Maintain a **presence registry** (e.g., Redis: `user_id → connection_server_id`) updated when users connect/disconnect. Server 1 looks up B → server 7, then forwards the message to server 7 via an internal message bus / **pub/sub** (publish to a channel server 7 subscribes to, or a direct RPC). Server 7 pushes it down B's WebSocket.

Also persist the message durably first (so it's not lost) and, if B is offline, store it as undelivered and deliver on reconnect (with read/delivery receipts). This connection-server + presence + pub/sub fan-out is the canonical chat architecture.
keyPoints: Look up B's server, forward via pub/sub / message bus
B's server pushes over its WebSocket
Persist message; queue + replay if B offline
followUps: How do you handle B being connected on two devices at once?
